title: Atmospheric Basics
intro: Every world with enough gravity wraps itself in gas. Find out what an atmosphere is and what it does, compare the very different air of Mercury, Venus, Earth, the Moon and Mars, and meet the trace gases that warm a planet through the greenhouse effect. Then learn to measure pressure, see why air thins with height and why warm air rises, how planets gain and lose their gas, how sunlight ionizes, breaks, scatters and warms the air (and why the sky is blue), and finish with the layers of Earth's atmosphere, why only Earth has a stratosphere, and how the magnetosphere shields us and lights the auroras.

learningObjectives.text: How does the greenhouse effect warm a planet?
Why do atmospheric properties vary with altitude?

sections.title: What an atmosphere is

img.alt: A deep blue sky with long wisps of white cloud above a flat blue sea.

steps.title: A blanket of gas held by gravity
bullets: An **atmosphere** is a layer of gas that surrounds a world and is held onto it by **gravity**.
Three questions run through this unit: what an atmosphere is, how the **greenhouse effect** warms a planet, and why the air changes with altitude.

img.alt: Four photos taken from the International Space Station showing thin glowing bands of green, orange and blue light along the edge of Earth against the black of space.

steps.title: Airglow: the atmosphere seen from orbit
bullets: From the International Space Station the atmosphere is a thin glowing band along Earth's edge.
The colourful glow (green, orange and blue) is called **airglow**: faint light given off by gas high in the atmosphere.

img.alt: Six views of Venus: an orange radar map of its surface, a pale cream true-colour globe hidden by cloud, a cut-away showing a metallic core, rocky mantle, crust, carbon dioxide atmosphere and sulfuric acid clouds, and three views in violet, infrared and ultraviolet light.

steps.title: Venus: a world hidden by its air
bullets: In visible light (true colour) Venus is a pale, featureless ball, because thick clouds hide the surface completely.
Radar passes through the clouds and maps the surface underneath. Pictures in violet, infrared and ultraviolet light show the cloud patterns.
Inside, Venus has a metallic core, a rocky mantle and a crust, wrapped in a carbon dioxide atmosphere with sulfuric acid clouds.

img.alt: A collage of weather on other worlds and in the sky: meteor streaks against the Milky Way, lightning, Jupiter's Great Red Spot, a swirling polar storm shown in red and cyan, and dark storm spots on blue Neptune.

steps.title: Weather on many worlds
bullets: Atmospheres support many kinds of weather: lightning, meteors burning up, and giant storms such as Jupiter's Great Red Spot and the dark spots on Neptune.

boxes.text: Gravity is what keeps the gas from drifting off into space. That is why small, low-gravity worlds struggle to keep an atmosphere.
Think of an atmosphere as a gas blanket tucked in by gravity.
An atmosphere is held by gravity, not by a magnetic field or by the planet's spin (pt1 slide 2). Venus's true-colour view shows only cloud tops; the surface map comes from radar (pt1 slide 3).

sections.title: What an atmosphere does

img.alt: Four cards: 1, pressure decides whether water is solid, liquid or gas; 2, light is absorbed and scattered, deciding which wavelengths reach the ground; 3, wind, weather and climate; 4, temperature, set by heat transport, albedo and the greenhouse effect.

steps.title: Four big effects
bullets: **Pressure** decides the physical state of substances on the surface, for example whether water can be a liquid.
Atmospheres **absorb and scatter light**, so they decide which wavelengths of light, if any, reach the surface.
They create **wind, weather and climate**.
They control a world's **temperature** through heat transport, albedo (how much light is reflected) and the greenhouse effect.

boxes.text: Without enough pressure, liquid water boils away or freezes. Air pressure is one reason Earth can have oceans.
P-L-W-T: Pressure, Light, Weather, Temperature.
The atmosphere does more than set temperature: pressure sets surface states, and it filters light (pt1 slide 7).

sections.title: Atmospheres of the terrestrial worlds

img.alt: Mercury, Venus, Earth, the Moon and Mars above a view of each surface, with the mass of each atmosphere: Mercury and the Moon about 10^4 kg, Venus 5 x 10^20 kg, Earth 5 x 10^18 kg and Mars 2.5 x 10^16 kg.

steps.title: A huge range of sizes
bullets: Atmospheres span a wide range of compositions and sizes.

Mercury and the Moon have almost no atmosphere (about 10^4 kg of gas). Venus's atmosphere (5 x 10^20 kg) is about **100 times** more massive than Earth's (5 x 10^18 kg). Mars has 2.5 x 10^16 kg, far less than Earth.

img.alt: Close-up of Mercury's grey, heavily cratered surface curving against a black sky.

steps.title: Mercury: a trace of gas
bullets: Mercury's atmosphere is extremely thin (tenuous), with trace amounts of hydrogen (H), helium (He), sodium (Na) and oxygen (O).

img.alt: The Moon's grey cratered surface under a completely black sky.

steps.title: The Moon: a trace of gas
bullets: The Moon's atmosphere is also extremely thin, with trace amounts of hydrogen (H), helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar).

img.alt: Pie chart of Venus's atmosphere: almost the whole circle is carbon dioxide, with a thin slice of molecular nitrogen.

steps.title: Venus: thick carbon dioxide
bullets: Venus has a very thick atmosphere made mostly of **carbon dioxide (CO₂)**: 96.5% CO₂ and 3.5% N₂.
Trace gases include SO₂, Ar, H₂O and CO.

img.alt: A colourised view of the surface of Venus: dark flat rocks under a uniformly yellow sky.

steps.title: The surface of Venus
bullets: A lander photographed a flat, rocky surface under a yellow-looking sky (the colours in the photo were added afterward).

img.alt: Pie chart of Earth's atmosphere: about three quarters molecular nitrogen, about one fifth molecular oxygen and a thin sliver of argon.

steps.title: Earth: nitrogen and oxygen
bullets: Earth has a moderately thick atmosphere made mostly of **molecular nitrogen (N₂)** and **molecular oxygen (O₂)**: 78.1% N₂, 20.9% O₂ and 0.93% argon (Ar).
Trace gases include CO₂, H₂O, neon and helium.

img.alt: A green field with yellow dandelions and trees under a blue sky streaked with thin white clouds in Calgary.

steps.title: Earth's blue sky
bullets: Our sky looks blue and the clouds white, as in this view over Calgary.

img.alt: Pie chart of Mars's atmosphere: almost all carbon dioxide, with small slices of molecular nitrogen and argon.

steps.title: Mars: thin carbon dioxide
bullets: Mars has a **thin** atmosphere made mostly of CO₂: 95% CO₂, 2.7% N₂, 1.9% Ar and 0.4% trace gases (O₂, H₂O).

img.alt: A wide panorama of Mars: reddish-brown rocky ground stretching to a hazy hill under a pale, dusty sky, with part of the rover in the corner.

steps.title: A Martian sunset
bullets: A rover's panorama shows Mars's dusty, pale sky over red rocky ground.

boxes.text: Venus and Mars both have CO₂ atmospheres, but Venus's is thousands of times more massive than Mars's. Earth's is different because life and oceans removed most of its CO₂ and added O₂.
Venus and Mars: 'mostly CO₂, a little N₂'. Earth: 'N-O-Ar' (nitrogen, oxygen, argon).

Venus's atmosphere is about 100x MORE massive than Earth's, not less (pt1 slide 4). Earth's main gas is nitrogen (78%), not oxygen (21%) (pt1 slide 10). Mars's thin air is still mostly CO₂, like Venus (pt1 slide 11). The sentence about Earth's air being changed by life and oceans in the 'why' box is outside the slides.

sections.title: Trace gases and greenhouse gases

img.alt: Table of trace gases in Earth's air with their amount, whether each is a pollutant and whether it is a greenhouse gas: carbon dioxide 420 ppm, water vapour 0 to 4%, ozone 1 ppm, methane 2 ppm, carbon monoxide 0.1 ppm, sulfur dioxide 1 ppb, halocarbons 1 ppb and noble gases 20 ppm.

steps.title: Small amounts that matter
bullets: Earth's air holds many gases in trace amounts: water vapour (H₂O), carbon dioxide (CO₂), ozone (O₃), pollutants and noble gases.
The **greenhouse gases** include **CO₂, H₂O, CH₄ (methane) and O₃ (ozone)**. They absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, which warms the planet through the greenhouse effect.
Some trace gases are pollutants but not greenhouse gases (carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide). Ozone, methane and halocarbons are both.

img.alt: Animation: yellow visible sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground; the ground gives off red infrared waves; greenhouse gas molecules absorb the infrared and send some of it back down, so the surface stays warmer.

steps.title: How the greenhouse effect works
bullets: Visible sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground.
The warm ground gives off **infrared** light.
Greenhouse gas molecules absorb that infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back down, so the surface ends up warmer than it would be without them.
Think of a **blanket**: it adds no heat of its own, it just slows the escape of heat. The energy still leaves to space in the end, only less directly.

img.alt: Bar chart of average surface temperature without and with the greenhouse effect: Venus -40 vs 470 degrees Celsius (510 degrees warmer), Earth -16 vs 15 (31 warmer), Mars -56 vs -50 (6 warmer). Mercury and the Moon get no greenhouse warming.

steps.title: How much warmer?
bullets: Without greenhouse gases, a world's average temperature would depend only on its **distance from the Sun** and its **reflectivity** (how much sunlight it bounces away).
**Earth** would average about **-16 °C** instead of **15 °C**: 31 °C of greenhouse warming, which keeps most water liquid.
**Venus** would be about **-40 °C** (its bright clouds reflect most sunlight) but is really about **470 °C**: over 500 °C of warming from its thick CO₂ air.
**Mars** gains only about **6 °C** (-56 to -50 °C) because its CO₂ air is so thin. **Mercury and the Moon** have no greenhouse warming at all.
N₂ and O₂ make up most of Earth's air but barely absorb infrared: molecules with just two atoms have few ways to vibrate and spin.

img.alt: Earth seen from orbit: towers of white cloud over a blue ocean, with a thin glowing blue line of air along the edge of the planet.

steps.title: Where the weather lives
bullets: The densest part of Earth's atmosphere is only about **10 km** thick, but the whole atmosphere reaches far higher. Most clouds and weather happen in this lowest layer.
Clouds are not steam and not a complicated mixture of gases: they are patches of air cool enough for **tiny water droplets to condense**.

img.alt: From the International Space Station, green aurora light swirls above clouds on Earth, with the station's solar panels in the corner.

steps.title: The top of the atmosphere
bullets: The International Space Station orbits at about **400 km**. Only about a **trillionth** of the atmosphere's mass lies above that height.
The upper boundary of the atmosphere crosses into space and the **magnetosphere**.

boxes.text: Greenhouse gases let visible sunlight in but slow the escape of infrared heat, like a blanket that lets light through.
Greenhouse gases: 'Can Water Make Ozone?' = CO₂, Water vapour, Methane, Ozone.

N₂ and O₂, the main gases, are NOT greenhouse gases (pt1 slide 12). CO₂ and water vapour are greenhouse gases but are not counted as pollutants in the table; carbon monoxide is a pollutant but NOT a greenhouse gas. Clouds are condensed water droplets, not steam (pt1 slide 13).

sections.title: Pressure and its units

img.alt: A force arrow labelled F pushing straight down on a flat area labelled A.

steps.title: Force spread over an area
bullets: **Pressure** is force divided by the area it acts on: **P = F / A**.
Its unit is the **pascal**: 1 Pa = 1 N/m² = 1 kg/(m·s²).
The same force on a smaller area gives a larger pressure.

img.alt: Pressure equals force divided by area; 1 pascal is 1 newton per square metre. 1 kPa is 1,000 Pa, 1 bar is 100,000 Pa, 1 atm is 101,325 Pa and 1 psi is 6,894.76 Pa. Sea level is about 1 atm (14.7 pounds per square inch); Calgary, about 1 km up, is about 0.88 atm, roughly 89 kPa.

steps.title: Other units
bullets: 1 kPa (kilopascal) = 1,000 Pa.
1 atm (atmosphere) = 101,325 Pa.
1 psi (pound per square inch) = 6,894.76 Pa.

img.alt: A round pressure gauge with two scales, kilopascals and pounds per square inch.

steps.title: Reading a gauge
bullets: Pressure gauges often show two scales at once, such as kilopascals and pounds per square inch.

boxes.text: Pressure, not total force, is what matters for gases: it tells you how hard the gas pushes on each square metre of anything it touches.
Kilo means a thousand: 1 kPa = 1,000 Pa. 'Bar' is a round 100,000 Pa; an atmosphere is a bit more, 101,325 Pa.
The deck writes 'Kpc' and '1 Pa = 101,325 Pa' (pt2 slide 1); these are typos for kPa and 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. Halving the area doubles the pressure; it does not halve it.

sourceNotes: Ch10.1 pt2 slide 1 (two typos corrected: 'Kpc' is kPa; '1 Pa = 101,325 Pa' is 1 atm = 101,325 Pa)

sections.title: Air pressure and altitude

img.alt: A tall stack of pillows beside a column of air molecules: the pillows at the bottom are squashed flat by the weight above, and the molecules are crowded at the bottom and spread out at the top.

steps.title: Pressure and density
bullets: Pressure and density are the **intensive** partners of force and mass: they describe the same property but do not depend on the size of the system.
That makes them useful for describing the atmosphere.

img.alt: A large glass jug of marbles with red arrows pushing in from the top, bottom, left and right toward one point in the middle.

steps.title: Pressure from every direction
bullets: Put your hand in a jar of marbles and you feel pressure from all directions, not just from the marbles above.
Air pressure likewise acts on your **whole body**. The force on an elephant is larger because it is bigger, but the **pressure** is the same.

steps.title: One atmosphere at sea level
bullets: The weight of the air above us gives about **1 atmosphere** of pressure at sea level, about **1.01 x 10^5 Pa** or **14.7 lb/in²**. Higher places have lower pressure.
In **Calgary**, about 1 km above sea level, the pressure is roughly **0.88 atm (89 kPa)**.

img.alt: Animation: a column of air with molecules crowded near the ground and spread out high up, marked high pressure below and low pressure above; beside it a bubble of air warmed by the ground rises, cools high up and sinks again in a loop.

steps.title: Squeezed air near the ground
bullets: Air can be compressed, so the air at low altitude is squashed by the air above and is much **denser**.
That is why it is harder to breathe at very high elevations: each breath holds fewer molecules.
Near the surface, the extra density raises the pressure above what it would be if air could not be compressed.

boxes.text: Each layer of air carries the weight of all the air above it, like the bottom pillow in a stack carrying all the others.
Stack of pillows: the bottom one is flattest. Air at the bottom is densest and has the highest pressure.

Pressure is the same on you and an elephant; only the total FORCE differs (pt2 slide 3). Calgary is LOWER pressure than sea level (0.88 atm), not higher (pt2 slide 4). The deck writes '89 kpc', meaning 89 kPa.

sections.title: The ideal gas law and convection

img.alt: Three balloons with arrows for moving air molecules: one balanced, one being blown up with more molecules and one heated by a candle so its molecules move faster; both of the last two expand.

steps.title: PV = nRT
bullets: Air roughly obeys the **ideal gas law**, PV = nRT (pressure x volume = amount of gas x a constant x temperature).
Raising the temperature T or the number of particles n raises the pressure P or the volume V. If nothing holds the air in, the **volume grows**.
A balloon stays inflated when the pressure inside and outside balance. Blowing in more air, or heating it so the molecules move faster, makes it expand until the pressures balance again.

img.alt: Animation: a column of air with molecules crowded near the ground and spread out high up, marked high pressure below and low pressure above; beside it a bubble of air warmed by the ground rises, cools high up and sinks again in a loop.

steps.title: Why warm air rises
bullets: Hotter air takes up more volume, so it is **less dense**. It rises, then cools at higher altitude and sinks again.
This cycle is **convection**, and it drives much of the weather.

boxes.text: Faster-moving molecules hit harder and more often, so warming a gas pushes its walls outward.
Hot air balloon: heat it, it swells, it floats.

Heating air with nothing holding it in increases its VOLUME (and lowers its density) rather than piling up pressure (pt2 slide 6). Warm air rises because it is less dense, not because heat itself 'rises'.

sections.title: How planets gain and lose atmospheres

img.alt: A volcano giving off a cloud of gas, and a pool of water with arrows rising from it into the air.

steps.title: Ways to gain gas
bullets: **Outgassing** from volcanoes.
**Evaporation** of surface liquid and **sublimation** of surface ice (ice turning straight into gas).

img.alt: Particles and wavy rays of light striking a surface and knocking material off it.

steps.title: More ways to gain gas
bullets: **Impacts of particles and photons** that knock atoms off the surface.
**Biological and human (anthropogenic) processes**, on Earth.

img.alt: Gas atoms in the upper air, some flying off upward; particles from above knocking atoms away; arrows of gas coming down into a pond and onto the ground.

steps.title: Ways to lose gas
bullets: **Thermal escape**: fast-moving atoms high up fly off into space.
**Sweeping by the solar wind**.
**Large impacts** blasting gas into space.
**Chemical reactions** with the surface, which lock gas into rock.
**Condensation** onto the surface (gas freezing or raining out).

img.alt: Two lists. Ways to gain gas: outgassing from volcanoes, evaporation and sublimation, impacts of particles and photons, and living things and people on Earth. Ways to lose gas: thermal escape, the solar wind, large impacts, chemical reactions with the surface and condensation onto the surface.

steps.title: Both lists side by side
bullets: Gains: outgassing, evaporation and sublimation, impacts of particles and photons, life and people.
Losses: thermal escape, solar wind, large impacts, chemical reactions, condensation.

boxes.text: An atmosphere is a balance: whatever a planet has today is what is left after billions of years of gains and losses.
Gains come up FROM the surface (volcanoes, evaporation); most losses go OUT to space or DOWN into the surface.

Impacts appear on both lists: small particle and photon impacts can ADD gas knocked off the surface, while large impacts can BLAST gas away (pt2 slides 7-8). Condensation and chemical reactions are losses, even though the gas stays on the planet.

sections.title: How sunlight affects an atmosphere

img.alt: Four kinds of light meeting molecules, from highest to lowest energy: X rays knock off an electron and break a molecule apart, ultraviolet breaks a molecule apart, visible light mostly passes straight through with blue scattered more than red, and infrared makes a molecule vibrate and rotate.

steps.title: Four things light can do to gas
bullets: **Ionization**: high-energy light knocks electrons out of atoms or molecules.
**Dissociation**: light breaks molecules apart.
**Scattering**: light bounces off in a new direction.
**Absorption and re-emission**: the energy is mostly turned into motion and heat, and the rest is given off again as a new photon.

steps.title: Which light does what
bullets: **X rays and ultraviolet** light can ionize and dissociate molecules.
Most **visible** light passes straight through, but nitrogen and oxygen molecules (N₂ and O₂) scatter **blue light at steeper angles than red light**.
**Greenhouse gas** molecules absorb **infrared** light, which makes them vibrate and rotate.

boxes.text: Higher-energy light can do more damage: X rays and UV have enough energy to break molecules, while infrared only sets them wiggling.
From high energy to low: X ray and UV 'break', visible 'bounces', infrared 'jiggles'.

Visible light is mostly TRANSMITTED, not absorbed (pt3 slide 1). It is infrared that greenhouse gases absorb, not visible light (pt3 slide 2). Ionization removes electrons; dissociation breaks molecules; they are not the same.

sourceNotes: Ch10.1 pt3 slides 1-2

images.alt: Four kinds of light meeting molecules, from highest to lowest energy: X rays knock off an electron and break a molecule apart, ultraviolet breaks a molecule apart, visible light mostly passes straight through with blue scattered more than red, and infrared makes a molecule vibrate and rotate.

sections.title: Why the sky is blue and sunsets are red

img.alt: Sunlight entering the atmosphere: blue light is scattered in all directions toward a person under a blue sky, while the remaining reddish light travels on to a person far away seeing a red sunset.

steps.title: Rayleigh scattering
bullets: Scattering by gas molecules depends on wavelength: **blue light scatters much more than red**. This is **Rayleigh scattering**.
Scattered blue light reaches your eyes from every part of the sky, so the **sky looks blue**.

img.alt: A sunset over a fjord: a deep blue sky overhead fading to bright orange and red near the horizon between snowy mountains.

steps.title: Red sunsets and sunrises
bullets: When the Sun is low, its light crosses much more air. Most of the blue is scattered out along the way, so the light that reaches you looks **red and orange**.

img.alt: A milky, bluish piece of glass on a white table with an orange glow in its shadow, where the light passing through has lost its blue.

steps.title: The same effect in a stone
bullets: A milky opal-like glass looks bluish from the side, and the light that passes through it comes out orange, for the same reason.

boxes.text: Short wavelengths are scattered most, so blue is spread across the sky while the direct beam keeps the reds.
Blue goes everywhere (the sky); red goes straight through (the sunset).

The sky is not blue because it reflects the ocean, and not because air is 'blue gas': it is Rayleigh scattering (pt3 slide 3). Sunsets are red because blue was REMOVED along the long path, not because red was added.

sections.title: Earth's atmospheric layers

img.alt: View from an airplane window: the wing over a sea of orange-lit clouds at sunset, with a thinner sky above.

steps.title: Layers set by temperature
bullets: All but the thinnest atmospheres have **layers**, told apart by how temperature changes with height.
The air gets thinner with altitude, but the temperature goes down and up.

img.alt: Graph of temperature against altitude in Earth's atmosphere with the lowest band, ground to about 12 km, boxed: the temperature falls from about 15 degrees Celsius at the ground to about minus 55, and a loop of rising warm air sits by the ground.

steps.title: Troposphere
bullets: The **lowest** layer, on average about **12 km** high.
Temperature **drops steadily** with altitude.
Almost **all weather** happens here.
It is warmed by **infrared light from the surface** and by **convection**.

img.alt: The same temperature graph with the band from about 12 to 80 km boxed: temperature rises to a peak near 0 degrees Celsius at about 50 km, then falls again, making a knee in the curve. Ultraviolet rays stop around 50 km.

steps.title: Stratosphere
bullets: Extends from about **20 km** to **50-85 km** (the upper part is sometimes called the **mesosphere**).
Temperature **rises** with altitude in the lower part and **drops** in the upper part, making a 'knee' in the graph.
The temperature peak matches the highest concentration of **ozone**, which absorbs **ultraviolet** light.

img.alt: The same graph with the band above about 80 km boxed: temperature climbs steeply with height, and the X-ray arrows stop in this layer.

steps.title: Thermosphere
bullets: Starts at about **85 km** and ends around **500 km**.
Temperature **rises steadily** with altitude because of more exposure to ionizing radiation and the **solar wind**.
UV light and X rays ionize and dissociate the few gas molecules up here, so this layer is the main part of the **ionosphere**.

img.alt: The same graph with the top band, around 500 km, boxed: the thinnest air, with a satellite drawn at that height.

steps.title: Exosphere
bullets: Starts at about **500 km** and gradually fades into space, ending around **10,000 km**.
Particles are so sparse that they rarely meet. Radiation can energize them enough to **escape into space**.

boxes.text: Each warm layer has its own heater: the ground's infrared warms the troposphere, ozone absorbing UV warms the stratosphere, and X rays and the solar wind heat the thermosphere.
'Tall Students Think Early': Troposphere, Stratosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere, from the bottom up.

Temperature does NOT just fall with height: it falls in the troposphere, rises then falls in the stratosphere, then rises in the thermosphere (pt3 slides 4-6). Weather is in the troposphere, not the stratosphere. The ionosphere is mainly the thermosphere. The slides give the troposphere as ~12 km but the stratosphere as starting 'about 20 km'; the graph shows the boundary near 12 km.

steps.title: Venus, Earth and Mars compared
bullets: **Venus** has a much **larger troposphere**, because its surface is much hotter.
Both Venus and Mars have **thermospheres and exospheres**.
**Earth is the only terrestrial planet with a stratosphere**, because only Earth has UV-absorbing **ozone (O₃)**.
The arrows on the graph show each planet's surface temperature if there were **no greenhouse effect**: Mars about -56 °C, Venus about -40 °C and Earth about -16 °C.

boxes.text: No ozone means nothing absorbs UV in the middle of the atmosphere, so there is no warm stratosphere bump on Venus or Mars.
Stratosphere = ozone = Earth only.

Venus and Mars DO have thermospheres and exospheres; only the stratosphere is missing (pt3 slide 8). Without a greenhouse effect Venus would be colder than freezing (-40 °C), even though it is closer to the Sun.

sections.title: The magnetosphere and auroras

img.alt: The solar wind streams from the Sun and bends around Earth's magnetic field, which is squashed on the Sun side and stretched into a long tail; aurora rings sit around the poles and charged particle belts circle the planet.

steps.title: A magnetic shield
bullets: Earth's **magnetosphere** protects the surface from charged particles streaming from the Sun, the **solar wind**.
The field is squashed on the side facing the Sun and stretched into a long tail on the far side. Belts of charged particles are trapped inside it.

img.alt: Green aurora curtains glowing over a dark forest under a starry sky.

steps.title: Auroras
bullets: Near the magnetic poles, the solar wind **energizes the thermosphere**, making it glow: the **auroras**.

boxes.text: Charged particles follow magnetic field lines, which dip down into the atmosphere near the poles, so that is where they hit the air.
No magnetic field, no shield: the solar wind can then strip away the upper atmosphere.
Auroras glow in the THERMOSPHERE near the magnetic poles, not in the troposphere where clouds are (pt3 slide 9). The magnetosphere stops charged particles, not sunlight.

cards.back: A layer of gas that surrounds a world and is held to it by gravity.
Faint coloured light (green, orange, blue) given off by gas high in Earth's atmosphere, seen as a glowing band from orbit.
cards.short: Glow of high gas seen from orbit

cards.front: What does an atmosphere's pressure decide?
cards.back: The physical state of substances on the surface, for example whether water can be liquid.
cards.short: Solid, liquid or gas on the surface

cards.back: How much light a surface or planet reflects. Together with heat transport and the greenhouse effect it helps set a world's temperature.

cards.front: Which worlds have almost no atmosphere?
cards.back: Mercury and the Moon: only trace amounts of gas, about 10^4 kg.

cards.front: How massive is Venus's atmosphere compared with Earth's?
cards.back: About 100 times more massive (5 x 10^20 kg versus 5 x 10^18 kg).
Hydrogen, helium, sodium and oxygen.
Hydrogen, helium, neon and argon.
Very thick: 96.5% carbon dioxide and 3.5% nitrogen, with traces of SO₂, Ar, H₂O and CO.
Moderately thick: 78.1% N₂, 20.9% O₂ and 0.93% Ar, with traces of CO₂, H₂O, Ne and He.
Thin: 95% CO₂, 2.7% N₂, 1.9% Ar and 0.4% trace gases (O₂, H₂O).
Gases that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, warming a planet: CO₂, H₂O, CH₄ and O₃.
Warming of a planet's surface because greenhouse gases absorb infrared light given off by the ground and re-emit some of it back down.

cards.front: Is carbon monoxide a greenhouse gas?
cards.back: No. It is a pollutant but not a greenhouse gas. Sulfur dioxide is the same.
Patches of air cool enough for microscopic water droplets to condense. They are not steam.

cards.front: How thick is the densest part of Earth's atmosphere?
cards.back: About 10 km. Most clouds and weather are in this layer.

cards.front: How much air is above the ISS (400 km)?
cards.back: Only about a trillionth of the atmosphere's total mass.
Force divided by the area it acts on: P = F / A.
The unit of pressure: 1 Pa = 1 N/m² = 1 kg/(m·s²).
A unit of pressure: 1 atm = 101,325 Pa, about the air pressure at sea level (14.7 lb/in²).
A unit of pressure equal to 100,000 Pa.
A property that does not depend on the size of the system. Pressure and density are the intensive partners of force and mass.
About 0.88 atm (89 kPa), because Calgary is about 1 km above sea level.

cards.front: Why is it harder to breathe high up?
cards.back: Air is compressible, so it is densest near the ground. High up it is thinner, so each breath holds fewer molecules.
PV = nRT. Raising temperature or the amount of gas raises the pressure or, if the gas is free to expand, the volume.
Warm air expands, becomes less dense and rises, then cools high up and sinks again.
Release of gas from a planet's interior by volcanoes; a main way to gain an atmosphere.
Ice turning directly into gas, one way a surface adds gas to the atmosphere.
Loss of gas when fast-moving atoms high in the atmosphere fly off into space.

cards.front: Five ways to lose an atmosphere
cards.back: Thermal escape, sweeping by the solar wind, large impacts, chemical reactions with the surface and condensation onto the surface.
Light knocking electrons out of atoms or molecules; caused by X rays and ultraviolet.
Light breaking molecules apart; caused by X rays and ultraviolet.
Light changing direction when it meets molecules. Nitrogen and oxygen scatter blue light more than red.
Wavelength-dependent scattering by gas molecules: blue scatters most, making the sky blue and sunsets red.
Lowest layer, average height about 12 km. Temperature drops with altitude, almost all weather happens here, warmed by surface infrared and convection.
About 20 km to 50-85 km. Temperature rises then falls (a 'knee'); the peak matches the most ozone, which absorbs UV.
About 85 to 500 km. Temperature rises steadily with altitude from X rays, UV and the solar wind; the main part of the ionosphere.
Starts about 500 km and fades into space by about 10,000 km. Particles rarely meet and can escape.
The region of Earth's magnetic field that shields the surface from the solar wind's charged particles.
cards.short: Magnetic shield from the solar wind

cards.back: Glowing light near the magnetic poles where the solar wind energizes the thermosphere.
The average temperature a world would have with no greenhouse warming, set only by its distance from the Sun and its reflectivity. Earth: -16 °C instead of 15 °C.

quiz.q: What holds an atmosphere onto a world?
quiz.why: An atmosphere is gas held to a world by gravity. Magnetic fields shield it from the solar wind but do not hold the gas down.

quiz.q: Which statement about the masses of the terrestrial atmospheres is correct?
options: Mars's is a little more than Earth's
Mercury's is about as large as Mars's
The Moon's is about as large as Earth's
quiz.why: Venus has about 5 x 10^20 kg of atmosphere and Earth about 5 x 10^18 kg, so Venus's is about 100 times more massive. Mars has less than Earth; Mercury and the Moon have only traces.

quiz.q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
quiz.why: Earth's air is 78.1% N₂, 20.9% O₂ and 0.93% Ar. CO₂ and water vapour are trace gases.

quiz.q: Which two worlds have atmospheres made mostly of carbon dioxide?
quiz.why: Venus is 96.5% CO₂ and Mars is 95% CO₂. Earth is mostly nitrogen, and Mercury and the Moon have only traces of other gases.

quiz.q: The Moon's very thin atmosphere contains traces of which gases?
quiz.why: The Moon has traces of H, He, Ne and Ar. Mercury's traces are H, He, Na and O.

quiz.q: Which list contains only greenhouse gases?
quiz.why: The greenhouse gases named are CO₂, H₂O, CH₄ and O₃. N₂, O₂ and Ar are not greenhouse gases, and CO and SO₂ are pollutants but not greenhouse gases.

quiz.q: Greenhouse gases warm a planet mainly by doing what?
options: Absorbing and re-emitting infrared light from the surface
Absorbing visible sunlight before it ever reaches the ground
Reflecting incoming sunlight straight back out to space
Blocking the charged particles of the solar wind
Ionizing the thin gas molecules high in the thermosphere
quiz.why: Visible light passes through and warms the ground; the ground gives off infrared, which greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit, partly back down.

quiz.q: According to the table of trace gases, which one is a pollutant but NOT a greenhouse gas?
quiz.why: Carbon monoxide (and sulfur dioxide) are pollutants but not greenhouse gases. Methane, ozone and halocarbons are both; CO₂ is a greenhouse gas but not listed as a pollutant.

quiz.q: What are clouds made of?
options: Steam rising off warm oceans and lakes
A complicated mixture of rare gases
Tiny water droplets condensed in cool air
Dust and smoke lifted off the ground
Pure water vapour, a white-coloured gas
quiz.why: Clouds are patches of air cool enough for tiny water droplets to condense. They are not steam or a special gas mix.

img.alt: Earth seen from orbit: towers of white cloud over a blue ocean, with a thin glowing blue line of air along the edge of the planet.

quiz.q: About how much of the atmosphere's mass lies above the International Space Station at 400 km?
quiz.why: Only about a trillionth of the atmosphere's mass lies above 400 km; the gas there is extremely thin but not entirely absent.

quiz.q: A force of 600 N presses on an area of 2 m². What is the pressure?

img.alt: A force arrow labelled F pushing straight down on a flat area labelled A.

quiz.q: How many pascals are in 1 atmosphere?
quiz.why: 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. 1 bar is 100,000 Pa, 1 kPa is 1,000 Pa and 1 psi is 6,894.76 Pa; 14.7 is atmospheric pressure in pounds per square inch.

quiz.q: The same force is spread over half the area. The pressure becomes:
quiz.why: P = F / A. Halving A with F unchanged doubles P.

quiz.q: Why do pressure and density work well for describing the atmosphere?
options: They are intensive: independent of size
They grow larger as the system grows
They stay the same at every altitude
They only apply to solids and liquids
They are measured in newtons and kilograms
quiz.why: Pressure and density are intensive partners of force and mass: the same property, but independent of the size of the system.

quiz.q: An elephant and a person stand side by side at sea level. Which is true?
options: Same pressure; more total force on the elephant
The air pressure on the person is greater
The air pressure on the elephant is greater
Both the pressure and the total force are equal
The air exerts no pressure on either of them
quiz.why: Air pressure is the same for both. The elephant has more surface, so the total force on it is larger.

img.alt: A large glass jug of marbles with red arrows pushing in from the top, bottom, left and right toward one point in the middle.

quiz.q: The air pressure in Calgary, about 1 km above sea level, is roughly:
quiz.why: Calgary's pressure is about 0.88 atm (89 kPa), less than the 1 atm at sea level because there is less air above.

quiz.q: Why is air near the ground much denser than air high up?
options: Air near the ground is colder, so it shrinks
Clouds push the air down toward the ground
Gravity is weaker near the ground than up high
Oxygen sinks to the bottom while nitrogen rises
Air is compressible; the air above squeezes it
quiz.why: Air can be compressed, so low air is squashed by everything above it and is denser. That is also why breathing is harder at high elevations.

quiz.q: By the ideal gas law PV = nRT, heating air that is free to expand will mainly:
options: Decrease its volume and make it denser
Increase its volume, so it is less dense
Increase its density as it heats up
Lower its temperature as it expands
Remove gas particles from the air
quiz.why: Raising T raises P or V; with nothing holding the air in, the volume grows, so the air becomes less dense and rises.

quiz.q: Which process ADDS gas to an atmosphere?
quiz.why: Outgassing adds gas. The other four are ways to lose gas.

quiz.q: Which process REMOVES gas from an atmosphere?
options: Evaporation of liquid on the surface
Sublimation of ice on the surface
quiz.why: Chemical reactions with surface rock lock gas away. Evaporation, sublimation, outgassing and life all add gas.

quiz.q: What does ionization mean?
options: Breaking a molecule into separate pieces
Making a molecule vibrate and rotate
Changing the direction a photon travels
Knocking electrons off atoms or molecules
Turning surface ice directly into gas
quiz.why: Ionization ejects electrons. Breaking molecules is dissociation; changing direction is scattering.

quiz.q: Which kind of light do greenhouse gas molecules absorb, making them vibrate and rotate?
quiz.why: Infrared photons are absorbed by greenhouse molecules, making them vibrate and rotate. X rays and UV ionize or dissociate; most visible light passes through.

quiz.q: Most visible light entering Earth's atmosphere:
options: Ionizes the oxygen molecules it meets
Passes through, though some is scattered
Is turned into infrared by the air
Is blocked by the ozone layer
quiz.why: Most visible photons are simply transmitted; some are scattered, blue more than red.

quiz.q: Why is the daytime sky blue?
options: N₂ and O₂ scatter blue more than red
Air reflects the blue of the oceans
Ozone absorbs the red part of sunlight
The Sun gives off mostly blue light
Water vapour in the air is blue
quiz.why: Rayleigh scattering: N₂ and O₂ scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths much more, so blue light comes at us from all over the sky.

quiz.q: Why do sunsets look red?
options: The light crosses more air and loses blue
Dust adds extra red light at sunset
The Sun itself cools down each evening
Ozone absorbs blue only at sunset
Clouds reflect red light from the ground
quiz.why: Near the horizon sunlight travels through much more air, so Rayleigh scattering removes most of the blue and the remaining light looks red and orange.

img.alt: A sunset over a fjord: a deep blue sky overhead fading to bright orange and red near the horizon between snowy mountains.

quiz.q: In which layer does almost all of Earth's weather happen?
quiz.why: The troposphere, the lowest layer (about 12 km), holds almost all weather.

img.alt: Graph of temperature against altitude in Earth's atmosphere with the lowest band, ground to about 12 km, boxed: the temperature falls from about 15 degrees Celsius at the ground to about minus 55, and a loop of rising warm air sits by the ground.

quiz.q: What causes the temperature peak (the 'knee') in the stratosphere?
options: Infrared given off by the ground
X rays arriving from the Sun
quiz.why: The peak matches the highest concentration of ozone, which absorbs ultraviolet light.

img.alt: The same temperature graph with the band from about 12 to 80 km boxed: temperature rises to a peak near 0 degrees Celsius at about 50 km, then falls again, making a knee in the curve. Ultraviolet rays stop around 50 km.

quiz.q: Which layer is the main region of the ionosphere?
quiz.why: In the thermosphere (about 85 to 500 km) UV and X rays ionize and dissociate the few molecules, making it the main part of the ionosphere.

img.alt: The same graph with the band above about 80 km boxed: temperature climbs steeply with height, and the X-ray arrows stop in this layer.

quiz.q: Why is Earth the only terrestrial planet with a stratosphere?
options: It is closest to the Sun
quiz.why: Ozone (O₃) absorbs UV and warms the stratosphere. Venus and Mars have no ozone layer, so no stratosphere, though both have thermospheres and exospheres.

img.alt: Temperature against altitude for Venus, Earth and Mars. Venus starts far hotter at the ground and cools over a deep troposphere; only Earth's curve has a warm bump near 50 km; Mars stays cold. Arrows mark each planet's surface temperature without a greenhouse effect: Mars -56, Venus -40 and Earth -16 degrees Celsius.

quiz.q: What produces the auroras?
options: Sunlight reflecting off the polar ice caps
Moonlight lighting clouds of water droplets
Ozone glowing in the stratosphere at night
Solar wind energizing the polar thermosphere
quiz.why: Charged particles from the solar wind energize the thermosphere near the magnetic poles, making it glow.

img.alt: The solar wind streams from the Sun and bends around Earth's magnetic field, which is squashed on the Sun side and stretched into a long tail; aurora rings sit around the poles and charged particle belts circle the planet.

quiz.q: Venus is closer to the Sun than Earth, yet its "no greenhouse" temperature (-40 °C) is lower than Earth's (-16 °C). Why?
options: Its slow rotation lets its night side freeze
It is farther from the Sun than Earth
It has no atmosphere to absorb sunlight
Its bright clouds reflect most of the sunlight that reaches it
Its carbon dioxide reflects infrared back to space
quiz.why: Without greenhouse warming, temperature depends only on distance and reflectivity. Venus's clouds reflect about 75% of sunlight, so it absorbs less than Earth. Its real 470 °C comes from a huge greenhouse effect.

img.alt: Bar chart of average surface temperature without and with the greenhouse effect: Venus -40 vs 470 degrees Celsius (510 degrees warmer), Earth -16 vs 15 (31 warmer), Mars -56 vs -50 (6 warmer). Mercury and the Moon get no greenhouse warming.

quiz.q: Which of the following worlds has the most substantial atmosphere?
quiz.why: Venus's atmosphere is about 100 times as massive as Earth's, with a surface pressure about 90 times greater. Mars's is thin, and the Moon and Mercury have almost none.

quiz.q: Which of the following planets has the least substantial atmosphere?
quiz.why: Mercury has only a trace of gas (about 10^4 kg in total). Mars's atmosphere is thin but still far more than Mercury's, and Neptune is a gas giant.

quiz.q: Approximately how much more massive is Venus's atmosphere than Mars's?
quiz.why: Venus has about 5 x 10^20 kg of air and Mars about 2.5 x 10^16 kg. 5 x 10^20 / 2.5 x 10^16 = 2 x 10^4, so about 10,000 times.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a way that atmospheres can lose mass?
options: Impactors can blast out material from both the surface and the atmosphere into space.
The solar wind can knock atmospheric particles into space.
Gravitational forces exerted by passing comets and asteroids can pull material off of the atmosphere of a planet.
Cool temperatures can cause atmospheric particles to condense into solids on a planet's surface.
quiz.why: Real loss processes are thermal escape, solar wind stripping, large impacts, condensation and chemical reactions with the surface. Passing comets and asteroids are far too small for their gravity to pull air away.

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly lists common pressure units in order of increasing magnitude?
options: 1 bar, 1 pound per square inch, 1 kilopascal, 1 atmosphere.
1 kilopascal, 1 pound per square inch, 1 atmosphere, 1 bar.
1 kilopascal, 1 pound per square inch, 1 bar, 1 atmosphere.
1 bar, 1 kilopascal, 1 atmosphere, 1 pound per square inch.
quiz.why: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa; 1 psi is about 6900 Pa; 1 bar = 100,000 Pa; 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. So kPa < psi < bar < atm.

quiz.q: Which of the following would decrease the pressure of an atmosphere?
options: Increasing the mass of the planet.
Exchanging heavier molecules for lighter ones.
quiz.why: Surface pressure is the weight of the air above. Lighter molecules make the same column weigh less. More particles, stronger gravity (a more massive planet) or higher temperature all raise pressure.

quiz.q: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as you go higher in altitude on Earth?
options: Temperature decreases with altitude and lower temperature tends to mean lower pressure.
Gravity gets much weaker with altitude.
The weight of the atmosphere above you decreases with altitude.
There are fewer greenhouse gases at higher altitude.
quiz.why: Pressure at any height comes from the weight of the air above it. The higher you go, the less air is left above you. Gravity barely changes over the height of the atmosphere.

quiz.q: What is a magnetosphere?
options: the layer of a planet in which its magnetic field is generated
the uppermost layer of any planetary atmosphere
a region of space around a planet in which the planet's magnetic field can trap charged particles
the region in a planet's atmosphere in which auroras occur
quiz.why: A magnetosphere is the region of space around a planet where its magnetic field controls charged particles, deflecting the solar wind and trapping some particles. The field is made in the core; auroras glow in the thermosphere.

quiz.q: Which of the following factors does NOT affect planetary temperature?
quiz.why: Temperature depends on distance from the Sun, albedo (reflectivity) and the atmosphere's greenhouse effect; tilt sets seasons and rotation sets how much the day and night sides differ. How long the orbit takes does not change how much sunlight arrives.

quiz.q: About what fraction of Earth's atmosphere is CO2?
quiz.why: CO2 is a trace gas on Earth, about 420 parts per million (0.04%). Earth's air is about 78% N2, 21% O2 and 1% Ar. 95% CO2 describes Mars and Venus.

quiz.q: Of the four gases CO2, H2O, N2, and O2, which are greenhouse gases?
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb infrared light. N2 and O2 have only two atoms and few ways to vibrate and spin, so they barely absorb infrared.

quiz.q: Which of the following gases absorbs ultraviolet light best?
quiz.why: Ozone (O3) is the strong ultraviolet absorber. That absorption heats Earth's stratosphere.

quiz.q: Rank these planets in order of the strength of the greenhouse effect on the planet, from the weakest to the strongest greenhouse effect.
quiz.why: Greenhouse warming: Mercury 0 °C (no atmosphere), Mars about 6 °C (thin CO2), Earth about 31 °C, Venus about 510 °C (thick CO2).

quiz.q: Which of the following correctly describes the greenhouse effect? (Each option ends the same way: eventually the temperature stabilizes because the heat lost rises rapidly with surface temperature.)
options: Sunlight heats up the Earth's surface, causing it to emit infrared wavelengths. Greenhouse gases in the troposphere act like the roof of a greenhouse, preventing convection from transporting the warm, infrared-heated air away from the surface, raising the surface temperature.
Sunlight heats up the Earth's surface, causing it to emit infrared wavelengths. Greenhouse gases slow down the escape of infrared radiation, so the surface temperature builds up.
Sunlight heats up the Earth's surface, causing it to emit infrared wavelengths. Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit a portion of this light back towards Earth, causing it to heat up further.

Sunlight heats up the Earth's surface, causing it to emit infrared wavelengths. Greenhouse gases absorb this light, heating up the atmosphere, which conducts thermal energy to the surface, increasing its temperature, too.
quiz.why: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared and re-emit it in random directions, which slows the escape of heat, like a blanket that adds no heat of its own. The 'roof stops convection' idea is how a real greenhouse works, not a planet. The re-emit option is close, but it implies the gases add heat rather than slow its escape; check which wording your instructor uses.

quiz.q: Which of the following lists the layers of a generic planetary atmosphere in the correct order from lowest to highest altitude?
quiz.why: From the ground up: troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone, only on Earth), thermosphere (absorbs X rays), exosphere (fades into space).

quiz.q: Why doesn't Mars have a stratosphere?
options: Its atmosphere does not contain enough of an ultraviolet-absorbing gas.
It lacks a strong enough magnetic field.
Its atmosphere does not contain enough greenhouse gases.
It is too small in size.
It is too far from the Sun.
quiz.why: A stratosphere forms where a gas such as ozone absorbs solar ultraviolet and warms that layer. Mars (and Venus) lack enough ozone, so neither has a stratosphere.

quiz.q: What is a stratosphere?
options: a part of the atmosphere that absorbs ultraviolet light
a lowest layer in the atmosphere
a part of the atmosphere that absorbs optical light
the highest layer in an atmosphere
a part of the atmosphere that absorbs x-rays
quiz.why: The stratosphere is the layer above the troposphere where ozone absorbs ultraviolet light, so temperature rises with height. X rays are absorbed higher, in the thermosphere.

quiz.q: What is the ionosphere?
options: a layer of the atmosphere that is above the exosphere
a layer of the atmosphere characterized by the presence of ozone
a portion of the troposphere in which ions are common
a portion of the thermosphere in which the gas is ionized
quiz.why: Solar X rays ionize gas in the thermosphere; that ionized region is the ionosphere. Ozone belongs to the stratosphere.

quiz.q: All the following statements are true. Which one explains why convection can occur in the troposphere but not in the stratosphere?
options: The stratosphere contains significant amounts of ozone but the troposphere does not.
Temperature declines with altitude in the troposphere but increases with altitude in the stratosphere.
Clouds tend to form in the troposphere but not the stratosphere.
Atmospheric pressure is much greater in the troposphere than in the stratosphere.
quiz.why: Convection needs warm air below cooler air, so the warm air can rise. In the troposphere it gets colder with height; in the stratosphere it gets warmer, so rising air stops.

order.title: Layers of Earth's atmosphere
order.prompt: Put the layers in order from the ground at the bottom to space at the top.
order.why: The troposphere is lowest (to about 12 km), then the stratosphere (to 50-85 km), the thermosphere (to about 500 km) and the exosphere (fading out by about 10,000 km).

order.title: Atmosphere mass
order.prompt: Order the worlds by the mass of their atmosphere, smallest at the bottom.
order.why: Mercury and the Moon have only traces (about 10^4 kg), Mars 2.5 x 10^16 kg, Earth 5 x 10^18 kg and Venus 5 x 10^20 kg.

order.title: Light, from strongest to weakest
order.prompt: Order these kinds of light by energy, lowest at the bottom.
order.why: Infrared has the least energy (it only makes molecules vibrate), then visible, then ultraviolet (breaks molecules), then X rays (knock off electrons and break molecules).

order.title: The greenhouse effect, step by step
order.prompt: Put the steps in order, first at the bottom.
order.why: Visible sunlight passes through the air, warms the ground, the ground gives off infrared, greenhouse gases absorb it and re-emit some back down, and the surface ends up warmer.

layers.name: Visible sunlight passes through the air
Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit it

sort.title: Greenhouse gas or not?
sort.prompt: Sort each gas by whether it is a greenhouse gas.
sort.why: CO₂, H₂O, CH₄, O₃ and halocarbons absorb infrared. N₂, O₂, the noble gases, CO and SO₂ do not.

sort.title: Gain or lose?
sort.prompt: Sort each process by whether it adds gas to an atmosphere or removes it.
sort.why: Gas comes from volcanoes, evaporation, sublimation, small impacts and life. It is lost by thermal escape, the solar wind, large impacts, reactions with rock and condensation.

sort.title: Which layer?
sort.prompt: Sort each fact into the layer it describes.

items.text: Warmed by infrared from the ground
Heated by X rays and the solar wind
Fades into space by about 10,000 km
Particles rarely meet and can escape

sort.why: Weather and cooling with height belong to the troposphere; ozone and the knee to the stratosphere (only on Earth); the ionosphere and auroras to the thermosphere; the faint edge where particles escape is the exosphere.

sourceNotes: Notes follow the three Ch10.1 decks in order (pt1 what an atmosphere is and the terrestrial atmospheres; pt2 pressure, gaining and losing gas; pt3 sunlight, layers, other planets and the magnetosphere).
Slide typos corrected in student text: 'Kpc' and 'kpc' mean kPa (pt2 slides 1, 4); '1 Pa = 101,325 Pa' means 1 atm = 101,325 Pa (pt2 slide 1).
Original diagrams (gen_*): effects of atmospheres, pressure units, gain and loss, layer summary, greenhouse animation, density and convection animation. No book figures are used.
